justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near 155.5 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 157.5 over the month. This trajectory assumes a continuation of the prevailing trend at the time of the forecast, with no major structural break in the underlying asset or indicator being tracked. The one-day estimate is anchored most heavily by recent price action and momentum, where short-term mean reversion tendencies and intraday patterns suggest limited movement from the last observed level. The weekly and monthly estimates incorporate a slight positive bias, likely reflecting a broader trend or fundamental backdrop that was marginally supportive, though not strongly so.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a standard reflection of increasing uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 8.6 units, consistent with typical daily volatility. By one week, that span grows to 17 units, and by one month it reaches 39 units. These widths were calibrated based on historical realized volatility at each respective horizon, scaled to account for the fact that uncertainty compounds non-linearly over time. Liquidity conditions, scheduled macro data releases, and any known event risk within each window also played a role in shaping how much room I gave on either side of the point estimate.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macro conditions — such as a sharper-than-anticipated inflation reading, a central bank policy surprise, or a sudden liquidity event — could drive the value well below the lower bound of the monthly interval at 138. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as better-than-expected earnings, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of geopolitical uncertainty could push the value above 177. These tail events are, by construction, excluded from a 90% interval, meaning there is still a meaningful 10% probability assigned to outcomes outside these bounds.

It is also worth noting that the one-month interval in particular carries model risk — the assumption that volatility and drift remain roughly stable over 30 days is fragile. Regime changes, correlation breakdowns, or sudden shifts in market sentiment can invalidate the statistical assumptions underlying the forecast. If the asset or variable in question is sensitive to binary event outcomes (such as regulatory decisions or geopolitical developments), the true distribution of outcomes may be bimodal or fat-tailed in ways that a symmetric confidence interval does not fully capture.
